claims.claim: 3D imaging showed the development of additional folds of the IGL perpendicular to the main fissures in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Nuclear TO-PRO-3 staining confirmed the altered fissure formation in P4 cerebellum and also showed the development of additional folds of the IGL perpendicular to the main fissures (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 2B showing additional folds in mutant cerebellum.

claims.claim: Despite the aberrant folds, CGNs and Purkinje cell lamination was grossly preserved in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Despite the aberrant folds, CGNs and Purkinje cell lamination was grossly preserved (Video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Video 1.

claims.claim: In P14 controls, cerebellar fissures were fully developed, the EGL was almost absent and IGL structure was very smooth and homogeneous.
claims.source: In P14 controls, cerebellar fissures were fully developed, the EGL was almost absent and IGL structure was very smooth and homogeneous (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3A showing normal P14 control cerebellum.

claims.claim: Plxnb2 mutants at P14 showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface.
claims.source: In contrast, Plxnb2 mutants showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface, an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations, and original fissures could not be defined easily (Figure 3B, Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3B and Video 2 showing ectopic CGN patches in P14 mutants.

claims.claim: Plxnb2 mutants at P14 showed an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations.
claims.source: In contrast, Plxnb2 mutants showed patches of CGNs remaining at the cerebellar surface, an IGL structure with many invaginations in different orientations, and original fissures could not be defined easily (Figure 3B, Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figure 3B and Video 2 showing aberrant IGL structure in P14 mutants.

claims.claim: The aberrant IGL structure and the patches of granule cells at the surface persisted in adulthood in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: The aberrant IGL structure and the patches of granule cells at the surface persisted in adulthood, well after cerebellar development was completed (Figure 3C,D, Video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Figures 3C and 3D and Video 3 showing persistent defects in P30 mutants.

claims.claim: All aberrant IGL folds in the Plxnb2 mutant were lined with a monolayer of Purkinje cells.
claims.source: All aberrant IGL folds in the Plxnb2 mutant were lined with a monolayer of Purkinje cells (Video 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 3D imaging data in Video 4 showing Purkinje cells lining IGL folds.

claims.claim: The Purkinje cell 'islets' observed in Plxnb2 mutant cerebellar sections correspond to stretches of Purkinje cells that line the heavily corrugated, but still continuous IGL.
claims.source: These 3D-data convey that the Purkinje cell 'islets' observed in Plxnb2 mutant cerebellar sections actually correspond to stretches of Purkinje cells that line the heavily corrugated, but still continuous IGL.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from 3D imaging data in Videos 3 and 4 showing the continuous nature of the Purkinje cell layer.

claims.claim: A limited, but significant reduction in cerebellar volume was observed throughout cerebellar development in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Because Plxnb2 mutant cerebella seemed to be smaller than controls on sections, we next analyzed the cerebellar volume in 3D. Indeed, a limited, but significant reduction was observed throughout cerebellar development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing reduced cerebellar volume at P4 and P30.

claims.claim: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects.
claims.source: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects and their performance on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod test data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing no significant difference between mutants and controls.

claims.claim: The performance of Plxnb2 mutants on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice.
claims.source: Plxnb2 mutant did not display any noticeable motor or behavioral defects and their performance on an accelerating rotarod was similar to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod test data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In controls, EdU+ CGN precursors were usually confined to the thin outer EGL (oEGL), whereas they were more dispersed in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: In controls, whereas EdU+ CGN precursors were usually confined to the thin outer EGL (oEGL), they were more dispersed in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data in Figure 4A showing dispersed EdU+ cells in mutant EGL.

claims.claim: The developing ML was much thinner in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: In addition, the developing ML was much thinner (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4A showing reduced ML thickness in mutants.

claims.claim: In control P9 cerebellum, Ki67 and Tag1 markers were segregated, whereas in Plxnb2 mutants, CGN precursors lost their confinement to the oEGL and intermingled with tangentially migrating Tag1+ CGNs in the iEGL.
claims.source: In control P9 cerebellum, both markers were segregated (Figure 4B), whereas in Plxnb2 mutants, CGN precursors lost their confinement to the oEGL and intermingled with tangentially migrating Tag1+ CGNs in the iEGL (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by double immunostaining data in Figure 4B showing intermingling of Ki67+ and Tag1+ cells in mutants.

claims.claim: No difference in the amount of EdU+ cells was detected for either 2 hr or 24 hr EdU administration in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: No difference in the amount of EdU+ cells was detected for either time of EdU administration, and there was no difference in the uptake of EdU by dividing cells over time (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4C showing similar EdU+ cell numbers in controls and mutants.

claims.claim: The quantification of the amount of EdU+ CGNs in the EGL that colocalized with Ki67 immunostaining did not show a difference in proliferation rate in Plxnb2-mutant brains.
claims.source: In addition, the quantification of the amount of EdU+ CGNs in the EGL (EdU injected 2 hr before brain collection) that colocalized with Ki67 immunostaining did not show a difference in proliferation rate in Plxnb2-mutant brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing similar EdU/Ki67 colocalization in controls and mutants.

claims.claim: A significant increase in the percentage of cells double-positive for EdU and H3P was observed in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed a significant increase in the percentage of cells double-positive for EdU and H3P (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 4D showing increased EdU+/H3P+ cells in mutants.

claims.claim: The cell cycle for Plxnb2 mutant CGNs is slightly longer.
claims.source: This implies that the cell cycle for Plxnb2 mutant CGNs is slightly longer.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased proportion of EdU+/H3P+ cells shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: There is probably no alteration of cell cycle progression in absence of Plexin-B2 although more experiments will be required to determine if the M phase is affected.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that there is probably no alteration of cell cycle progression in absence of Plexin-B2 although more experiments will be required to determine if the M phase is affected.
claims.evidence: The claim is a cautious interpretation of the data in Figure 4, acknowledging the need for further experiments.

claims.claim: 99.6% of all targeted GFP+ cells in the cerebellum were CGNs and co-expressed Pax6 after in vivo electroporation.
claims.source: With this method 99.6% of all targeted GFP+ cells in the cerebellum were CGNs and co-expressed Pax6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing GFP/Pax6 colocalization.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in the length of the processes extended by tangentially migrating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: By comparing the initial steps of postmitotic CGN development, we found a significant reduction in the length of the processes (and future parallel fibers) extended by tangentially migrating CGNs in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5D showing shorter bipolar leading and trailing processes in mutants.

claims.claim: Cell body size and shape for proliferating and tangentially migrating CGNs was similar in both Plxnb2 mutant and control genotypes.
claims.source: Cell body size and shape for proliferating and tangentially migrating CGNs was similar in both genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing similar cell body width/length ratios.

claims.claim: GFP+ CGN precursors intermingled with migrating bipolar CGNs in the EGL of Plxnb2 mutant animals.
claims.source: As implied by the EdU and Ki67/Tag1 immunohistochemistry (Figure 4A,B), we observed that GFP+ CGN precursors intermingled with migrating bipolar CGNs in the EGL of Plxnb2 mutant animals (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5C showing mixed distribution of multipolar and bipolar GFP+ CGNs in mutant EGL.

claims.claim: Multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutant were spread throughout the EGL and bipolar CGNs sometimes even resided in the ML.
claims.source: Indeed, quantification of the location of multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the outer, inner EGL or ML, shows that multipolar and bipolar CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutant were spread throughout the EGL and that bipolar CGNs sometimes even resided in the ML (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing altered distribution of CGN morphologies in mutants.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, a fraction of the bipolar and tangentially migrating GFP+ CGNs were also labeled with EdU administered 2 hr before fixation.
claims.source: Intriguingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, a fraction of the bipolar and tangentially migrating GFP+ CGNs, were also labeled with EdU (which only labels dividing cells), administered 2 hr before fixation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5C and 5E showing EdU+ bipolar GFP+ CGNs in mutants.

claims.claim: Only a very small fraction of tangentially migrating bipolar GFP+ CGNs were EdU+ in controls.
claims.source: By contrast, only a very small fraction of tangentially migrating bipolar GFP+ CGNs were found in controls (Figure 5C,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5E showing low percentage of EdU+ bipolar cells in controls.

claims.claim: Some of the bipolar GFP+/EdU+ CGNs were indeed proliferating as shown by H3P co-expression.
claims.source: When combining the EdU staining with H3P to mark acutely dividing cells, we could confirm that, although rare, some of the bipolar GFP+/EdU+ were indeed proliferating (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing GFP+/EdU+/H3P+ cells in mutants.

claims.claim: Some bipolar GFP+ CGNs co-expressed H3P and Tag1 in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Some bipolar GFP+ CGNs also co-expressed H3P and Tag1 (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5F showing GFP+/H3P+/Tag1+ cells in mutants.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, the CGN switch from proliferation to tangential migration is altered and these two phases are not spatio-temporally separated anymore.
claims.source: This suggests that in Plxnb2 mutants, the CGN switch from proliferation to tangential migration is altered and that these two phases are not spatio-temporally separated anymore.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 5C-F showing proliferating bipolar CGNs in mutants.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in the proportion of CGNs that had initiated radial migration 48 hr after electroporation in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: To further support this hypothesis, we next analyzed GFP+ CGNs 48 hr after electroporation. Again, there was a significant reduction in the proportion of CGNs that had initiated radial migration in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5G showing fewer radial CGNs and more tangential CGNs in mutants at 2 days post-electroporation.

claims.claim: Plxnb2-deficient CGNs might remain longer in both their proliferative and tangential phases.
claims.source: This, together with the slight delay in M-phase (Figure 4D), suggest that Plxnb2-deficient CGNs might remain longer in both their proliferative and tangential phases.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 4D and 5G showing delayed cell cycle and migration progression.

claims.claim: As soon as Plxnb2 mutant CGNs started radial migration, their morphology closely resembled that of control CGNs.
claims.source: As soon as Plxnb2 mutant CGNs started radial migration, their morphology closely resembled that of control CGNs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing similar process lengths in radially migrating CGNs.

claims.claim: Differences in leading process length were no longer observed in radially migrating Plxnb2 mutant CGNs.
claims.source: Differences in leading process length were no longer observed, and their ascending axons in the ML were of comparable length (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing similar leading process and axon lengths in radial CGNs.

claims.claim: During radial migration, CGN cell bodies had a slightly more circular shape in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Conversely, during radial migration, CGN cell bodies had a slightly more circular shape in Plxnb2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing increased width/length ratio in mutant radial CGNs.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, CGNs in the IGL acquired their stereotypical CGN morphology slightly faster than in controls.
claims.source: Moreover, in Plxnb2 mutants, CGNs in the IGL acquired their stereotypical CGN morphology with a cell body of 7–8 μm in diameter bearing 3–4 claw-shaped primary dendrites, slightly faster than in controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G showing more mutant CGNs with 4 dendrites at P20.

claims.claim: In the IGL, CGNs might differentiate faster in Plxnb2 mutants than in controls.
claims.source: Together, this suggests that in the IGL, CGNs might differentiate faster in Plxnb2 mutants than in controls.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G showing accelerated dendrite pruning in mutants.

claims.claim: After completion of cerebellar development, Plxnb2 mutant CGNs displayed strikingly disorganized parallel fibers.
claims.source: After completion of cerebellar development, Plxnb2 mutant CGNs displayed strikingly disorganized parallel fibers (Figure 5H, Videos 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H and Videos 5 and 6 showing disorganized parallel fibers in adult mutants.

claims.claim: Instead of being restricted to a thin sub-layer of the ML in controls, parallel fibers were more spread out in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Instead of being restricted to a thin sub-layer of the ML in controls, parallel fibers were more spread out in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H showing dispersed parallel fibers in mutants.

claims.claim: Some CGN axons were completely misprojecting deep into the cerebellar white matter in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: Some CGN axons were even completely misprojecting deep into the cerebellar white matter where they run along myelinated Purkinje cell axons and mossy fibers (Figure 5F and F-II and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing CGN axons in the white matter.

claims.claim: The ectopic CGN axons in the white matter did not get myelinated in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: The ectopic CGN axons keep some of their normal characteristics since they did not get myelinated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B showing unmyelinated GFP+ axons in the white matter.

claims.claim: In the IGL of Plxnb2 mutants, the labeled CGNs were more dispersed, and some formed patches at the cerebellar surface.
claims.source: In the IGL of Plxnb2 mutants, the labeled CGNs were more dispersed, and some formed patches at the cerebellar surface (Figure 5G and HIII).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5H showing ectopic CGN patches at the surface.

claims.claim: According to the 'stacking model', developing parallel fibers accumulate in the ML in an inside-out time sequence, with CGNs born later extending parallel fibers above those of earlier born CGNs.
claims.source: According to the 'stacking model', developing parallel fibers accumulate in the ML in an inside-out time sequence, with CGNs born later extending parallel fibers above those of earlier born CGNs (Espinosa and Luo, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Espinosa and Luo, 2008.

claims.claim: The dispersion of proliferating CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutants EGL together with the presence of proliferation markers in tangentially migrating CGNs suggest that their developmental clock is perturbed.
claims.source: The dispersion of proliferating CGNs in the Plxnb2 mutants EGL together with the presence of proliferation markers in tangentially migrating CGNS, suggest that their developmental clock is perturbed.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from data in Figures 4 and 5 showing mixed proliferating and migrating CGNs in mutants.

claims.claim: Plxnb2 mutant parallel fibers were much more scattered across the ML.
claims.source: Accordingly, Plxnb2 mutant parallel fibers were much more scattered across the ML.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 6A showing dispersed parallel fibers in mutants.

claims.claim: GFP+ and Tomato+ parallel fibers were clearly segregated in control mice.
claims.source: As expected, GFP+ and Tomato+ parallel fibers were clearly segregated in control mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6A showing segregated early and late-born parallel fibers in controls.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, parallel fibers lost the inside-out organization in the ML.
claims.source: Strikingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, parallel fibers lost this inside-out organization in the ML (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6A showing overlapping early and late-born parallel fibers in mutants.

claims.claim: At P11, early GFP+ fibers occupied a space within the ML twice larger than in controls and largely overlap with later-born Tomato+ parallel fibers in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: At P11, early GFP+ fibers occupied a space within the ML twice larger than in controls and largely overlap with later-born Tomato+ parallel fibers, which were also more spread than in controls (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6A showing increased ML occupancy by GFP+ and tdTom+ fibers in mutants.

claims.claim: In controls, nascent parallel fibers normally extend at the base of the iEGL, just above the tips of developing Purkinje dendritic arbors.
claims.source: In controls (left panel), nascent parallel fibers normally extend at the base of the iEGL, just above the tips of developing Purkinje dendritic arbors (yellow arrowheads).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers at the EGL/ML border in controls.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutant, parallel fibers extend throughout the EGL and cross the Purkinje dendrites in the ML.
claims.source: However, in Plxnb2 mutant (right panel) parallel fibers extend throughout the EGL and cross the Purkinje dendrites in the ML (yellow arrowheads indicate the tips of Purkinje dendrites).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers throughout the ML in mutants.

claims.claim: In P9 Plxnb2 mutants, the young GFP+ parallel fibers ran throughout the entire ML between the Purkinje cell dendrites, which in turn appeared disorganized and more branched than controls.
claims.source: In P9 Plxnb2 mutants, the young GFP+ parallel fibers ran throughout the entire ML between the Purkinje cell dendrites, which in turn appeared disorganized and more branched than controls.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing disorganized Purkinje dendrites in mutants.

claims.claim: In Plxnb2 mutants, Vglut1+ synapses extended to the tip of the Purkinje cell dendrites at P9.
claims.source: Interestingly, in Plxnb2 mutants, Vglut1+ synapses extended to the tip of the Purkinje cell dendrites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing increased Vglut1 density at distal dendrites in mutants.

claims.claim: The ratio between Vglut1+ puncta at the distal ends and the proximal base of the dendritic arbor was significantly higher in Plxnb2 mutants at P9.
claims.source: We quantified the ratio between Vglut1+ puncta (fluorescent integrated density) at the distal ends and the proximal base of the dendritic arbor, and found significantly more synapses on the distal end compared to control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing increased distal/proximal Vglut1 ratio in mutants.

claims.claim: At later stages, no difference could be observed in the distribution of CGN-Purkinje synapses between controls and Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.source: At later stages, no difference could be observed in the distribution of CGN-Purkinje synapses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing similar Vglut1 distribution at P30.

claims.claim: In controls, nascent parallel fibers extended at the bottom of the iEGL just above the tips of Purkinje dendrites.
claims.source: In controls, nascent parallel fibers extended at the bottom of the iEGL just above the tips of Purkinje dendrites Plxnb2 mutant brains.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fiber position in controls.

claims.claim: At P9, the Purkinje cells in the Plxnb2 mutant seem underdeveloped and developing parallel fibers cross the entire ML.
claims.source: Where at P9, the Purkinje cells in the Plxnb2 mutant seem underdeveloped and developing parallel fibers cross the entire ML (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6B showing parallel fibers throughout the ML in P9 mutants.

claims.claim: New parallel fibers crisscrossing deep into the ML were found in P13 Plxnb2 mutant.
claims.source: New parallel fibers crisscrossing deep into the ML were also found in P13 Plxnb2 mutant, when the ML is much larger and the Purkinje dendrites are more developed (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 6C showing parallel fibers deep in the ML in P13 mutants.

claims.claim: CGNs exiting EGL explants follow a developmental sequence closely resembling in vivo CGNs.
claims.source: As previously described, CGNs exiting the explants follow a developmental sequence closely resembling in vivo CGNs (Kawaji et al., 2004; Kerjan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kawaji et al., 2004 and Kerjan et al., 2005.

claims.claim: CGN precursors divide inside the explant or close to it in EGL explant cultures.
claims.source: As in the oEGL, CGN precursors divide inside the explant or close to it (see below and Yacubova and Komuro, 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yacubova and Komuro, 2002 and by data in Figure 10 showing dividing cells near explants.

claims.claim: After plating, postmitotic cells become bipolar, grow long neurites and migrate away from the explant by nuclear translocation, as during tangential migration in the iEGL.
claims.source: After plating, postmitotic cells become bipolar, grow long neurites and migrate away from the explant by nuclear translocation, as during tangential migration in the iEGL (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7A showing bipolar CGN migration from explants.

claims.claim: Two to 3 days after plating, CGNs start aggregating and form satellites around the explant.
claims.source: Two to 3 days later, CGNs start aggregating and form satellites around the explant (Figure 7A; Kawaji et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7A and citation to Kawaji et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The cells migrating away from the explant were CGNs as confirmed by Pax6 immunostaining.
claims.source: Immunocytochemical analysis of young explants with Pax6, a marker for pre-and postmitotic CGNs, confirmed that the cells migrating away from the explant were CGNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A showing Pax6+ cells migrating from explants.

claims.claim: Although the explant contained GFAP+ glial cells extending processes outward, their cell bodies seldom left the explant.
claims.source: Although the explant contained GFAP+ glial cells extending processes outward, their cell bodies seldom left the explant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing GFAP+ cells confined to explants.

claims.claim: DAPI-stained nuclei from Plxnb2 mutant CGNs stayed closer to the explant compared to controls.
claims.source: We next compared explants from P4-5 Plxnb2fl/fl or En1Cre;Plxnb2fl/fl EGL after 1 day in vitro (DIV) and noticed a difference in outward CGN migration. DAPI-stained nuclei from Plxnb2 mutant CGNs stayed closer to the explant (Figure 7B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figures 7B and 7C showing reduced migration distance in mutant explants.

claims.claim: β-III tubulin staining revealed shorter and more fasciculated neurites in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: Furthermore, β-III tubulin staining revealed a difference in neurite outgrowth (Figure 7B), with shorter and more fasciculated neurites in Plxnb2 mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 7B showing altered neurite morphology in mutant explants.

claims.claim: Almost all GFP+ cells were positive for CGN markers such as Pax6 and Sema6A in EGL explant cultures.
claims.source: Almost all GFP+ cells were positive for CGN markers such as Pax6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and Sema6A (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B), and did not resemble GFAP+ glial cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C showing GFP+ cells are CGNs.

claims.claim: At DIV1 in Plxnb2 mutant explant cultures, the proportion of multipolar GFP+ CGNs was significantly increased.
claims.source: Strikingly, at DIV1 in Plxnb2 mutant explant cultures, the proportion of multipolar GFP+ CGNs was significantly increased (65.42 ± 2.37% in mut vs. 48.88 ± 2.65% in ctl, MWU(353) p<0.0001) and the proportion of bipolar cells was decreased (Figure 7D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7E showing increased multipolar cells in mutant explants at DIV1.

claims.claim: By DIV2 almost all cells – control or mutant – had a bipolar morphology in EGL explant cultures.
claims.source: However, by DIV2 almost all cells – control or mutant – had a bipolar morphology (Figure 7D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7E showing most cells are bipolar at DIV2.

claims.claim: DIV1 bipolar Plxnb2 mutant CGNs had shorter processes than control cells in EGL explant cultures.
claims.source: Interestingly, as observed in vivo (Figure 5C), DIV1 bipolar Plxnb2 mutant CGNs had shorter processes than control cells (Figure 7D,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7F showing shorter leading and trailing processes in mutant bipolar CGNs.

claims.claim: At DIV2, Plxnb2 mutant had a higher proportion of GFP+ CGNs that were not attached to the explant.
claims.source: Finally, bipolar cells could be further subdivided into two categories: cells that connected with their trailing process to the original explant, and cells that were disconnected from the explant. Interestingly, at DIV2, Plxnb2 mutant had a higher proportion of GFP+ CGNs that were not attached to the explant (Figure 7D,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 7G showing more detached bipolar cells in mutants at DIV2.

claims.claim: Control GFP+ CGNs usually migrated away from the explant in a straight and radial direction, whereas Plxnb2 mutant GFP+ CGNs sometimes reversed direction one or even multiple times during the acquisition period.
claims.source: Interestingly, whereas control GFP+ CGNs usually migrated away from the explant in a straight and radial direction, Plxnb2 mutant GFP+ CGNs sometimes reversed direction one or even multiple times during the acquisition period (Figure 8A, Video 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 8A and Video 7 showing altered migration patterns in mutants.

claims.claim: The speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed in Plxnb2 mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: Although the speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed (Figure 8B), both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction (moving back toward the explant) were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 8B showing similar migration velocity in controls and mutants.

claims.claim: Both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs.
claims.source: Although the speed of migrating bipolar CGNs was not changed (Figure 8B), both the relative amount of distance and time going in negative direction (moving back toward the explant) were significantly increased in Plxnb2 mutant CGNs (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 8C showing increased reverse movement in mutant CGNs.

claims.claim: In fixed DIV1 cultures, Plxnb2 mutant CGN nuclei appear closer to the explant probably because they spend more time moving in reverse direction.
claims.source: These results probably explain why in fixed DIV1 cultures, Plxnb2 mutant CGN nuclei appear closer to the explant (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the time-lapse data in Figure 8 showing increased reverse movement in mutants.

claims.claim: Both in vivo and in vitro data support an abnormal outgrowth of processes in Plxnb2-deficient tangentially migrating CGNs.
claims.source: Taken together, both our in vivo and in vitro data support an abnormal outgrowth of processes in Plxnb2-deficient tangentially migrating CGNs.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary inference from data in Figures 5 and 7 showing shorter processes in mutant tangentially migrating CGNs.

claims.claim: There was a much lower amount of DAPI nuclei visible around DIV1 Plxnb2 mutant explants compared to controls.
claims.source: Although there was a much lower amount of DAPI nuclei visible around the explant (Figure 9A,B), a similar amount of EdU+ nuclei was observed (Figure 9A,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data in Figure 9B showing fewer DAPI+ cells around mutant explants.

claims.claim: A similar amount of EdU+ nuclei was observed around DIV1 control and Plxnb2 mutant explants.

results.result: Plexin-B2 is specifically expressed in proliferating CGN precursors in the outer EGL and is downregulated as CGNs become postmitotic and begin tangential migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C52-C54 are strongly supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1A-C), in situ hybridization (Figure 1F), and co-labeling with proliferation markers (EdU) and postmitotic markers (Tag1). The temporal and spatial restriction of Plexin-B2 expression is well-documented.

results.result: Plexin-B2 deletion causes severe disorganization of cerebellar cortex lamination and foliation, including ectopic CGN patches, intermingled parallel fibers, and aberrant Purkinje cell dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C6-C8, C32, C55, C59-C62 are supported by extensive imaging data from null mutants (Figure 1D) and conditional knockouts (Figures 1F-H, 2, 3, 6). The phenotype is consistently observed across multiple genetic models and developmental stages, with quantitative and qualitative evidence.

results.result: Conditional deletion of Plexin-B2 using En1Cre and Wnt1-Cre lines phenocopies the null allele, demonstrating cell-autonomous function in CGN precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C60, C163-C164 are supported by in situ hybridization (Figure 1F), immunostaining (Figure 1G), and phenotypic comparison (Figure 1H). The conditional knockouts show complete loss of Plexin-B2 in the EGL and reproduce the cerebellar defects, confirming cell-autonomous action.

results.result: Plexin-B2 mutants show delayed cerebellar fissure formation starting at birth, with fissures remaining shallow and additional aberrant folds developing perpendicular to main fissures.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are supported by developmental time-course imaging (Figure 2A) and 3D light-sheet microscopy (Figure 2B). The delayed fissure formation is evident at P0 and persists through P4, with quantitative documentation of the aberrant folding patterns.

results.result: The disorganized cerebellar structure in Plexin-B2 mutants, including ectopic CGN patches and corrugated IGL lined by continuous Purkinje cell layer, persists into adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are supported by 3D imaging at P14 and P30 (Figures 3A-D, Videos 2-4). The data demonstrate that developmental defects are permanent, with the 3D analysis revealing that Purkinje cell 'islets' are actually continuous stretches lining the corrugated IGL.

results.result: Cerebellar volume is modestly but significantly reduced in Plexin-B2 mutants throughout development, indicating that neuronal generation is largely unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C79 and C173 are supported by quantitative 3D volumetric analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) showing statistically significant but limited reduction (~15%) at P4 and P30. This supports the interpretation that cell generation is not severely impaired.

results.result: Plexin-B2 mutants show no overt motor deficits as assessed by rotarod performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by rotarod testing data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) showing no significant difference between mutants and controls across three consecutive days. However, more sensitive behavioral assays might reveal subtle deficits.

results.result: In Plexin-B2 mutants, proliferating CGN precursors escape the oEGL and intermingle with postmitotic tangentially migrating CGNs in the iEGL.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C82-C84, C93-C94 are supported by EdU labeling (Figure 4A), Ki67/Tag1 double immunostaining (Figure 4B), and GFP electroporation studies (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). The spatial segregation of proliferating and migrating CGNs is clearly disrupted.

results.result: Overall CGN proliferation rate is not significantly altered in Plexin-B2 mutants based on EdU incorporation and Ki67 colocalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C89 are supported by quantitative analysis of EdU+ cells at 2hr and 24hr (Figure 4C) and EdU/Ki67 colocalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). However, claim C89 appropriately notes that more experiments are needed to fully assess M-phase, indicating appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The proportion of EdU+/H3P+ double-positive cells is significantly increased in Plexin-B2 mutants, suggesting a slightly longer cell cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by quantitative data (Figure 4D) showing increased EdU+/H3P+ cells in mutants. The interpretation of a longer cell cycle is reasonable but should be confirmed with additional cell cycle analysis methods.

results.result: Tripolar electrode in vivo electroporation efficiently and specifically targets CGNs, with 99.6% of GFP+ cells co-expressing the CGN marker Pax6.
results.evaluation: Claims C90 and C165 are supported by quantitative colocalization data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). This validates the method for studying individual CGN morphology and demonstrates high specificity for CGN targeting.

results.result: Tangentially migrating bipolar CGNs in Plexin-B2 mutants have significantly shorter leading and trailing processes compared to controls, both in vivo and in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C91 and C138 are supported by quantitative morphometric analysis in vivo (Figure 5D) and in explant cultures (Figure 7F). The consistent finding across both systems strengthens the conclusion about altered process outgrowth.

results.result: Cell body size and shape of proliferating and tangentially migrating CGNs are similar between Plexin-B2 mutants and controls.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by quantitative width/length ratio measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). This indicates that Plexin-B2 specifically affects process outgrowth rather than overall cell morphology.

results.result: In Plexin-B2 mutants, a significant fraction of tangentially migrating bipolar CGNs remain mitotically active, indicating altered temporal separation of proliferation and migration phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99, C174 are supported by EdU labeling (Figure 5C, E), EdU/H3P colocalization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), and H3P/Tag1 double labeling (Figure 5F). The data clearly demonstrate proliferating bipolar CGNs in mutants, a rare occurrence in controls.

results.result: Plexin-B2 mutant CGNs show delayed progression from tangential to radial migration, with fewer cells initiating radial migration 48 hours post-electroporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101, C194 are supported by quantitative analysis of CGN developmental stages at 2 days post-electroporation (Figure 5G). The data show significantly more tangential and fewer radial CGNs in mutants, supporting delayed developmental progression.

results.result: Once Plexin-B2 mutant CGNs initiate radial migration, their morphology and process lengths are comparable to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by morphometric analysis of radially migrating CGNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). This indicates that Plexin-B2 function is primarily required during the proliferative and tangential migration phases.

results.result: Radially migrating CGN cell bodies are slightly more circular in Plexin-B2 mutants compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by width/length ratio measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). While statistically significant, the biological significance of this subtle morphological difference is unclear.

results.result: CGNs in the IGL of Plexin-B2 mutants acquire their mature morphology slightly faster than controls, with more cells having 4 dendrites at P20.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by quantitative dendrite analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G). This suggests potential compensatory acceleration of differentiation once CGNs reach the IGL, though the mechanism is unclear.

results.result: Adult Plexin-B2 mutant CGNs display severely disorganized parallel fibers that are dispersed throughout the molecular layer, with some axons misprojecting into white matter while remaining unmyelinated.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 are supported by imaging of adult electroporated cerebella (Figure 5H, Videos 5-6, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B). The data demonstrate persistent axonal disorganization and ectopic projections, with confirmation that mislocalized axons retain their unmyelinated character.

results.result: The developmental clock of CGNs is perturbed in Plexin-B2 mutants, leading to loss of inside-out parallel fiber organization in the molecular layer, with early and late-born fibers extensively overlapping.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by dual electroporation experiments (Figure 6A) showing that early-born (GFP+) and late-born (tdTomato+) parallel fibers lose their normal spatial segregation in mutants. This demonstrates disruption of the temporal organization of parallel fiber layering.

results.result: In Plexin-B2 mutants, nascent parallel fibers extend throughout the EGL and deep into the molecular layer, crossing Purkinje cell dendrites rather than remaining at the EGL/ML border.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120, C125-C126 are supported by imaging at P9 and P13 (Figures 6B-C). The data show that parallel fibers in mutants fail to respect normal laminar boundaries, extending aberrantly through the developing molecular layer.

results.result: At P9, Vglut1+ synapses extend to the distal tips of Purkinje cell dendrites in Plexin-B2 mutants, but this difference normalizes by P30.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by Vglut1 immunostaining and quantification (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B). The transient alteration in synapse distribution suggests developmental compensation, though the mechanism is unclear.

results.result: EGL explant cultures predominantly contain CGNs (Pax6+, Sema6A+) with minimal glial contamination, validating the culture system for studying CGN development.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132, C135 are supported by immunocytochemistry (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C). The high purity of CGN cultures validates the explant system for mechanistic studies.

results.result: In explant cultures, Plexin-B2 mutant CGNs migrate shorter distances from the explant and extend shorter, more fasciculated neurites compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134, C188 are supported by DAPI nuclear distribution analysis (Figure 7B-C) and β-III tubulin staining (Figure 7B). The reduced migration distance is consistent with in vivo observations and prior studies (Maier et al., 2011).

results.result: At DIV1, Plexin-B2 mutant explants show a significantly increased proportion of multipolar CGNs, but by DIV2 most cells in both genotypes have adopted bipolar morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137, C152-C153 are supported by quantitative morphological analysis at DIV1 and DIV2 (Figure 7E, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B). The data indicate delayed morphological transition in mutants that eventually resolves.

results.result: At DIV2, Plexin-B2 mutant cultures have a higher proportion of bipolar CGNs that are detached from the explant.
results.evaluation: Claim C139 is supported by quantification of attached vs. detached bipolar cells (Figure 7G). This suggests altered adhesion or premature detachment during migration in mutants.

results.result: Plexin-B2 mutant bipolar CGNs show altered migration directionality with increased reverse movement toward the explant, though overall migration speed is unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C143, C191 are supported by time-lapse imaging and quantitative tracking (Figure 8A-C, Video 7). The data demonstrate that mutant CGNs alternate between forward and reverse movement, explaining their reduced net displacement despite normal velocity.

results.result: DIV1 Plexin-B2 mutant explants show fewer total DAPI+ cells but similar numbers of EdU+ and EdU+/H3P+ cells compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 are supported by quantitative cell counting (Figure 9A-D). The discrepancy between total cell numbers and proliferating cell numbers suggests altered migration dynamics rather than proliferation defects in the explant system.

results.result: At DIV1, multipolar cells show high EdU incorporation, suggesting they are proliferating CGN precursors that have escaped from the explant.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 are supported by EdU labeling data (Figure 9F). The high proportion of EdU+ multipolar cells supports their identity as proliferating precursors, consistent with in vivo observations.

results.result: At DIV2, Plexin-B2 mutant cultures show significantly more EdU+ bipolar cells, suggesting that bipolar cells continue to be generated from proliferating precursors longer than in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C151 are supported by EdU labeling at DIV2 (Figure 9G). This indicates prolonged or asynchronous generation of postmitotic CGNs in mutant cultures, consistent with disrupted developmental timing.

results.result: Time-lapse imaging confirms that multipolar cells are proliferating CGN precursors that divide to produce bipolar daughter cells that commence tangential migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C155 are supported by time-lapse imaging showing cell division (Figure 10A, Video 8). This directly demonstrates the precursor identity of multipolar cells and validates their role in the developmental sequence.

results.result: Plexin-B2 mutant multipolar CGN precursors show strikingly increased motility, covering twice the cumulative distance of control precursors before division.
results.evaluation: Claims C156, C190, C192 are supported by quantitative tracking of multipolar cells (Figures 10C-D). The increased motility of precursors is a novel finding that suggests Plexin-B2 normally restricts precursor movement.

results.result: The increased number of multipolar cells in mutant explants likely explains the higher number of observed cell divisions per explant.
results.evaluation: Claim C157 is supported by correlation between multipolar cell numbers (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B) and division counts (Figure 10F). This is a reasonable inference though the relationship could be more directly tested.

results.result: After cytokinesis, Plexin-B2 mutant daughter cells take significantly longer to adopt bipolar morphology and appear highly motile during this transition period.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C159 are supported by time-lapse analysis (Figure 10E, Video 8). The delayed polarization after division suggests Plexin-B2 may have a role in post-mitotic morphological maturation or cytokinesis completion.

results.result: Plexin-B2 might function in cytokinesis, as suggested by delayed M-phase progression, prolonged multipolar state, and comparison to its role in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C176-C178, C186 are speculative interpretations based on indirect evidence (increased EdU+/H3P+ cells, delayed bipolarity after division) and analogies to other systems. While the hypothesis is plausible and supported by citations to relevant literature, direct evidence for cytokinesis defects (e.g., binucleate cells, midbody abnormalities) is lacking. Additional experiments are needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: Plexin-B2 restricts CGN motility and controls the timing of CGN differentiation, with its downregulation required for proper segregation of postmitotic CGNs from cycling precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C160-C161, C187, C199, C224 represent the major conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the collective evidence showing increased motility in mutants (Figures 8, 10), altered developmental timing (Figures 4-5, 9), and loss of spatial segregation (Figures 4-5). The conclusions appropriately synthesize the experimental findings.

results.result: The molecular mechanisms downstream of Plexin-B2 in CGN development remain unclear, though Rap1 GTPases are proposed as potential key partners based on their properties and roles in other neuronal systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C223 discuss potential ligands and downstream signaling partners. While the discussion is well-informed by literature (multiple citations), it is largely speculative regarding the specific mechanisms in CGNs. The proposal that Rap1 GTPases are the main partners (C220) is a reasonable hypothesis but lacks direct experimental support in this study. The discussion appropriately acknowledges these uncertainties.

results.result: Background information on plexin biology, cerebellar anatomy, CGN development, and prior Plexin-B2 knockout studies establishes the context for the current work.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C48 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge and set up the rationale for the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: The current study confirms and extends prior findings on Plexin-B2 function, showing that mutant CGNs follow the normal developmental sequence but with altered timing and spatial organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C163, C169-C172 summarize how the current work relates to prior studies. These are supported by the data presented and appropriate citations. The study successfully builds on prior work by providing cellular-level analysis that was previously lacking.

results.result: The tripolar electrode electroporation method offers advantages over MADM and viral approaches for studying CGN development, including the ability to perform multiple rounds of electroporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C168 are supported by successful application of the method (Figures 5-6) and appropriate citations comparing to alternative approaches. The demonstration of dual electroporation (Figure 6A) validates the claimed advantage for studying temporal aspects of development.

results.result: The abnormal association of proliferation and migration together with excessive motility likely explains the cerebellar foliation and layering defects, with potential connections to Zeb1 transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C225-C227 provide a mechanistic synthesis supported by the data and appropriate citations. Claim C228 is a reasonable speculation for future work. The connection between cellular phenotypes and tissue-level organization is well-argued, though the Zeb1 connection remains to be tested.
